claim: RNA splicing is an essential part of eukaryotic gene expression.
source: RNA splicing is an essential part of eukaryotic gene expression.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of splicing in eukaryotic biology.

claim: Splicing occurs in the range of minutes.
source: Splicing occurs in the range of minutes and is limited by the speed of RNA polymerase elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Splicing is limited by the speed of RNA polymerase elongation.
source: Splicing occurs in the range of minutes and is limited by the speed of RNA polymerase elongation.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of donor bond half-lives in relation to intron length and transcription rates.

claim: Splicing kinetics strongly depends on the position and nature of nucleotides flanking splice sites.
source: Splicing kinetics strongly depends on the position and nature of nucleotides flanking splice sites, and on structural interactions between unspliced RNA and small nuclear RNAs in spliceosomal intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by the single nucleotide models and their predictive power for bond half-lives.

claim: Splicing kinetics depends on structural interactions between unspliced RNA and small nuclear RNAs in spliceosomal intermediates.
source: Splicing kinetics strongly depends on the position and nature of nucleotides flanking splice sites, and on structural interactions between unspliced RNA and small nuclear RNAs in spliceosomal intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between predicted nucleotide effects and known RNA-RNA interactions in spliceosome structures.

claim: The 'yield' of splicing is the efficiency of converting unspliced to spliced RNA.
source: Finally, we introduce the 'yield' of splicing as the efficiency of converting unspliced to spliced RNA and show that it is highest for mRNAs and independent of splicing kinetics.
evidence: This is a definition introduced by the authors in this study.

claim: Splicing yield is highest for mRNAs.
source: Finally, we introduce the 'yield' of splicing as the efficiency of converting unspliced to spliced RNA and show that it is highest for mRNAs and independent of splicing kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B comparing splicing yields across RNA classes.

claim: Splicing yield is independent of splicing kinetics.
source: Finally, we introduce the 'yield' of splicing as the efficiency of converting unspliced to spliced RNA and show that it is highest for mRNAs and independent of splicing kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis showing that yield and rate are distinct aspects of splicing.

claim: Splicing is a two-step reaction that results in the removal of introns from precursor RNA and the formation of mature RNA with joined exons.
source: Splicing is a two-step reaction that results in the removal of introns from precursor RNA and the formation of mature RNA with joined exons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the splicing mechanism.

claim: Splicing is catalyzed by the spliceosome.
source: Splicing is catalyzed by the spliceosome, a dynamic ribonucleoprotein machine assembled from small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complexes (snRNPs) and several non-RNP factors (Herzel et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The spliceosome is a dynamic ribonucleoprotein machine assembled from small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complexes (snRNPs) and several non-RNP factors.
source: Splicing is catalyzed by the spliceosome, a dynamic ribonucleoprotein machine assembled from small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complexes (snRNPs) and several non-RNP factors (Herzel et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In metazoa, the majority of introns are excised by the major spliceosome.
source: In metazoa, the majority of the introns are excised by the major spliceosome, whereas a minority is removed by the minor spliceosome (Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A minority of introns in metazoa is removed by the minor spliceosome.
source: In metazoa, the majority of the introns are excised by the major spliceosome, whereas a minority is removed by the minor spliceosome (Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spliceosomes are recruited through conserved RNA elements including the 5´-splice site at the exon-intron border (donor site), the 3´-splice site at the intron-exon border (acceptor site), and the branch point.
source: Spliceosomes are recruited through conserved RNA elements, the 5´-splice site at the exon-intron border (donor site), the 3´-splice site at the intron-exon border (acceptor site), and the branch point, which is followed by a polypyrimidine track (Coolidge et al., 1997; Turunen et al., 2013) and located ~18–40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the acceptor site (Ruskin and Green, 1985; Ruskin et al., 1985; Taggart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The branch point is followed by a polypyrimidine track.
source: Spliceosomes are recruited through conserved RNA elements, the 5´-splice site at the exon-intron border (donor site), the 3´-splice site at the intron-exon border (acceptor site), and the branch point, which is followed by a polypyrimidine track (Coolidge et al., 1997; Turunen et al., 2013) and located ~18–40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the acceptor site (Ruskin and Green, 1985; Ruskin et al., 1985; Taggart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The branch point is located ~18–40 nucleotides upstream of the acceptor site.
source: Spliceosomes are recruited through conserved RNA elements, the 5´-splice site at the exon-intron border (donor site), the 3´-splice site at the intron-exon border (acceptor site), and the branch point, which is followed by a polypyrimidine track (Coolidge et al., 1997; Turunen et al., 2013) and located ~18–40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the acceptor site (Ruskin and Green, 1985; Ruskin et al., 1985; Taggart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Additional RNA sequences such as splicing enhancers and silencers are found in both introns and exons and can influence the choice between splice sites.
source: Additional RNA sequences such as splicing enhancers and silencers are found in both introns and exons and can influence the choice between splice sites (Zhu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Assembly of the major spliceosome begins with recognition of the donor site by U1 snRNP.
source: Assembly of the major spliceosome begins with recognition of the donor site by U1 snRNP (Kondo et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 1980; Seraphin and Rosbash, 1989; Zhuang and Weiner, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The U2 auxiliary factor binds to the poly-pyrimidine track and the acceptor site, generating the E complex.
source: The U2 auxiliary factor then binds to the poly-pyrimidine track and the acceptor site (Valcárcel et al., 1996; Zamore and Green, 1989; Zamore et al., 1992) generating the E complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: U2 snRNP binding to the branchpoint results in the A complex.
source: U2 snRNP then binds the branchpoint, resulting in the A complex (Konarska and Sharp, 1986; Perriman and Ares, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the A complex, U1 snRNA binds the donor site and U2 snRNA binds the branchpoint.
source: In the A complex, U1 snRNA binds the donor site and U2 snRNA binds the branchpoint, rendering the branchpoint adenosine base available for interaction with the acceptor site (Berglund et al., 2001; Query et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Binding of the U4/U5/U6 tri-snRNP leads to the B complex.
source: Binding of the U4/U5/U6 tri-snRNP leads to the B complex (Bertram et al., 2017a), which is first activated (Bact) and then converted to the catalytically active B* complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the B* complex, the donor site is positioned close to the branchpoint in a RNA network formed between the precursor RNA and U2, U5 and U6 snRNAs.
source: In the B* complex, the donor site is positioned close to the branchpoint in a RNA network formed between the precursor RNA and U2, U5 and U6 snRNAs (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the first step of splicing, the 2´-hydroxyl group of the branchpoint adenosine serves as a nucleophile to attack the donor site and to generate a cleaved 5´-exon and the lariat intermediate.
source: In the first step, the 2´-hydroxyl group of the branchpoint adenosine serves as a nucleophile to attack the donor site and to generate a cleaved 5´-exon and the lariat intermediate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the splicing mechanism.

claim: The first step of splicing leads to the C complex.
source: This leads to the C complex (Zhan et al., 2018) that is then rearranged to form the C* complex, which is catalytically active to carry out the second step.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the C* complex, the ends of exons to be joined are juxtaposed.
source: In the C* complex, the ends of exons to be joined are juxtaposed (Bertram et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2017), and this enables the 3´-hydroxyl group of the last nucleotide of the 5´-exon to attack the acceptor site, leading to exon ligation and excision of the intron lariat.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the second step of splicing, the 3´-hydroxyl group of the last nucleotide of the 5´-exon attacks the acceptor site, leading to exon ligation and excision of the intron lariat.
source: In the C* complex, the ends of exons to be joined are juxtaposed (Bertram et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2017), and this enables the 3´-hydroxyl group of the last nucleotide of the 5´-exon to attack the acceptor site, leading to exon ligation and excision of the intron lariat.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the splicing mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The P complex contains the ligated exons, which are subsequently released, completing the splicing process.
source: The resulting P complex contains the ligated exons, which are subsequently released, completing the splicing process (Bai et al., 2017; Wilkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vivo splicing happens mainly co-transcriptionally, when newly transcribed RNA is still attached to RNA polymerase II and chromatin.
source: Although biochemical assays show that splicing can occur in the absence of transcription, in vivo splicing happens mainly co-transcriptionally, when newly transcribed RNA is still attached to RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and chromatin (for review see Alexander and Beggs, 2010; Bentley, 2014; Saldi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Compromising Pol II transcription elongation increases alternative splicing.
source: Furthermore, compromising Pol II transcription elongation increases alternative splicing (de la Mata et al., 2003; Dujardin et al., 2014; Ip et al., 2011; Pagani et al., 2003), providing evidence that an optimal elongation rate is essential for a co-transcriptional splicing (Davis-Turak et al., 2018; Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: An optimal elongation rate is essential for co-transcriptional splicing.
source: Furthermore, compromising Pol II transcription elongation increases alternative splicing (de la Mata et al., 2003; Dujardin et al., 2014; Ip et al., 2011; Pagani et al., 2003), providing evidence that an optimal elongation rate is essential for a co-transcriptional splicing (Davis-Turak et al., 2018; Fong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing that compromising elongation affects splicing.

claim: Native elongating transcript sequencing in human cells (NET-seq) indicates that splicing occurs soon after introns are synthesized.
source: Native elongating transcript sequencing in human cells (NET-seq) indicates that splicing occurs soon after introns are synthesized (Mayer et al., 2015; Nojima et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using NET-seq.

claim: In yeast, splicing is 50% complete when Pol II is 45 nt downstream the acceptor splice site.
source: Further, the combination of single molecule intron tracking (SMIT) and long read sequencing in yeast shows that splicing is 50% complete when Pol II is 45 nt downstream the acceptor spice site (Oesterreich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: Different estimates for splicing rates have been reported, ranging from 15 to 30 s to 4.3-10 min per splicing event.
source: Such studies led to very different splicing rate estimates, ranging from 15 to 30 s (Huranová et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2013; Rino et al., 2014) to 4.3-10 min (Coulon et al., 2014; Schmidt et al., 2011; Singh and Padgett, 2009) per splicing event.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies with different methodologies.

claim: Discrepancies in splicing rate estimates may stem from differences in methods used, selection of genes studied, and variance in intron lengths.
source: These discrepancies may stem from the difference in methods used, which can introduce perturbations, from the selection of genes studied, and from the great variance in intron lengths between human genes.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for discrepancies in previous studies.

claim: The 'splicing efficiency' is typically defined by the ratio of spliced over unspliced RNAs at steady state.
source: In particular, the 'splicing efficiency' is typically defined by the ratio of spliced over unspliced RNAs at steady state (Braberg et al., 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature defining this metric.

claim: The ratio of spliced over unspliced RNAs has been successfully employed to study RNA stability.
source: However, the same ratio has been successfully employed to study RNA stability, with the assumption that unspliced RNA levels reflect RNA synthesis and spliced RNA levels reflect the ratio of RNA synthesis over degradation (Gaidatzis et al., 2015; Zeisel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using this ratio for stability analysis.

claim: Sequencing new transcripts from chromatin-associated RNA fractions compared to cytoplasmic fractions led to splicing rate estimates from 43 s to 15–120 min per splicing event.
source: To overcome the limitations of steady-state transcriptome sequencing, one approach is to sequence new transcripts from chromatin-associated RNA fractions and compare them to cytoplasmic fractions, which led to splicing rate estimates from 43 s (Davis-Turak et al., 2015) to 15–120 min (Bhatt et al., 2012; Pandya-Jones et al., 2013) per splicing event.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using this approach.

claim: 4sU-seq coupled with kinetic modeling obtained median splicing rate estimates of 6.7 min or 14 min per splicing event in human cells.
source: Others have used 4sU-seq and similar approaches to obtain median splicing rate estimates in human cells of 6.7 min (Mukherjee et al., 2017) or 14 min (Rabani et al., 2014) per splicing event.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using 4sU-seq.

claim: 4sU-seq introduces biases when applied to the human system because the obtained data are artificially biased toward pre-existing 5'-regions of the RNA due to the length of human genes.
source: However, 4sU-seq also introduces biases when applied to the human system because the obtained data are artificially biased toward pre-existing 5'-regions of the RNA due to the length of human genes (Schwalb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study identifying this bias.

claim: TT-seq was performed after different 4sU-labeling time points in human K562 cells.
source: To study kinetics of splicing in vivo, we performed TT-seq (Schwalb et al., 2016) after different 4sU-labeling time points in human K562 cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: The TT-seq protocol includes RNA fragmentation before 4sU-labeled RNA is purified and sequenced.
source: In contrast to 4sU-seq, the TT-seq protocol includes RNA fragmentation before 4sU-labeled RNA is purified and sequenced.
evidence: This describes a key methodological difference of TT-seq.

claim: RNA fragmentation in TT-seq eliminates 5' regions of nascent RNAs that were already transcribed and spliced prior to incorporation of the label, thus removing the 5'-bias.
source: This is a crucial step that eliminates 5' regions of nascent RNAs that were already transcribed, and spliced, prior to incorporation of the label, and thus removes the 5'-bias.
evidence: This explains the advantage of TT-seq over 4sU-seq for avoiding 5' bias.

claim: On average, 250 million 150-nucleotide paired-end reads were obtained for each TT-seq sample.
source: On average, we obtained 250 million and 55 million 150-nucleotide (nt) paired-end reads for each of the TT-seq and RNA-seq samples, respectively.
evidence: This describes the sequencing depth obtained in the experiments.

claim: On average, 55 million 150-nucleotide paired-end reads were obtained for each RNA-seq sample.
source: On average, we obtained 250 million and 55 million 150-nucleotide (nt) paired-end reads for each of the TT-seq and RNA-seq samples, respectively.
evidence: This describes the sequencing depth obtained in the experiments.

claim: The experiments were highly reproducible.
source: The experiments were highly reproducible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: TT-seq signals covered both introns and exons in transcribed regions.
source: Visual inspection of the mapped reads revealed strong TT-seq signals in transcribed regions covering both introns and exons (Figure 1B), whereas RNA-seq data covered mainly exons (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of coverage tracks shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNA-seq data covered mainly exons.
source: Visual inspection of the mapped reads revealed strong TT-seq signals in transcribed regions covering both introns and exons (Figure 1B), whereas RNA-seq data covered mainly exons (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of coverage tracks shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The relative number of intronic reads in TT-seq data decreased with 4sU-labeling time.
source: The relative number of intronic reads in TT-seq data decreased with 4sU-labeling time, whereas the signal for exons increased.
evidence: This observation is consistent with the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The signal for exons in TT-seq data increased with 4sU-labeling time.
source: The relative number of intronic reads in TT-seq data decreased with 4sU-labeling time, whereas the signal for exons increased.
evidence: This observation is consistent with the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spliced introns are more rapidly degraded than exons that are maintained in mature, stable RNA.
source: These observations were consistent with capture of newly synthesized precursor RNA because spliced introns are more rapidly degraded than exons that are maintained in mature, stable RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of intronic and exonic reads over time.

claim: 341,855 putative introns were found using a threshold of at least 10 split reads for an exon-exon boundary.
source: Using a threshold of at least 10 split reads for an exon-exon boundary, we found 341,855 putative introns (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the number of introns identified in the analysis.

claim: The relative number of non-split reads compared to split reads was highest after 2 min of 4sU-labeling and progressively decreased with longer labeling times.
source: The relative number of these non-split reads compared to split reads was highest after 2 min of 4sU-labeling and progressively decreased with longer labeling times, eventually converging to a similar coverage as in the RNA-seq samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Coverage with split reads decreased with the distance to the transcription start site in 4sU-seq data but not in TT-seq data.
source: Coverage with split reads decreased with the distance to the transcription start site (TSS) in 4sU-seq data but not in TT-seq data (Figure 1C, data from Schwalb et al., 2016), suggesting that the previously reported estimation of splicing rates with 4sU-seq (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Rabani et al., 2014), overestimated splicing rates for 5' introns compared to 3' introns.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing 4sU-seq and TT-seq.

claim: Previously reported estimation of splicing rates with 4sU-seq overestimated splicing rates for 5' introns compared to 3' introns.
source: Coverage with split reads decreased with the distance to the transcription start site (TSS) in 4sU-seq data but not in TT-seq data (Figure 1C, data from Schwalb et al., 2016), suggesting that the previously reported estimation of splicing rates with 4sU-seq (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Rabani et al., 2014), overestimated splicing rates for 5' introns compared to 3' introns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed 5' bias in 4sU-seq data.

claim: About one half of the putative introns (177,322) mapped to splice sites that had been annotated in GENCODE.
source: About one half of the putative introns (177,322) mapped to splice sites that had been annotated in the database of transcribed regions GENCODE (Materials and methods), whereas the other half did not (164,533).
evidence: This describes the proportion of identified introns that were previously annotated.

claim: More than 99% of putative introns not previously annotated in GENCODE represented introns ending with the GT|AG canonical dinucleotides.
source: Of these putative introns that had not been previously annotated as splice sites in GENCODE, more than 99% represented introns ending with the GT|AG canonical dinucleotides.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the newly identified introns.

claim: 21% of non-annotated putative introns represented new combinations of already annotated donors and acceptors.
source: Moreover, 21% represented new combinations of already annotated donors and acceptors (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 18% of non-annotated putative introns map to a non-annotated donor site and to a previously annotated acceptor site.
source: Furthermore, 18% map to a non-annotated donor site and to a previously annotated acceptor site, 22% to a non-annotated acceptor site and to a previously annotated donor site.
evidence: This describes the distribution of newly identified splice sites.

claim: 22% of non-annotated putative introns map to a non-annotated acceptor site and to a previously annotated donor site.
source: Furthermore, 18% map to a non-annotated donor site and to a previously annotated acceptor site, 22% to a non-annotated acceptor site and to a previously annotated donor site.
evidence: This describes the distribution of newly identified splice sites.

claim: 38% of non-annotated putative introns mapped to both non-annotated donor sites and non-annotated acceptor sites.
source: Interestingly, another 38% mapped to both non-annotated donor sites and non-annotated acceptor sites.
evidence: This describes the proportion of completely novel splice junctions.

claim: About one half of introns with both non-annotated donor and acceptor sites was located within an annotated GENCODE gene (intronic).
source: Of these, about one half was located within an annotated GENCODE gene (intronic), whereas the other half was located in regions of the genome not annotated in GENCODE (intergenic).
evidence: This describes the genomic location of novel splice junctions.

claim: The number of splice sites has previously been underestimated.
source: Overall, this analysis indicates that the number of splice sites has previously been underestimated, in agreement with recent studies that integrated very large datasets of the public RNA-seq repository (Nellore et al., 2016) or studies that used full-length mRNA sequencing (Anvar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the large number of newly identified splice sites, supported by citations to similar findings.

claim: The study modeled the steady-state rates of synthesis and degradation of three different phosphodiester bonds individually: the exon-intron bond at the donor site, the intron-exon bond at the acceptor site, and the bond between the two joined exons after exon ligation.
source: Following this idea, we modeled the steady-state rates of synthesis and degradation (or equivalently cleavage) of each of three different phosphodiester bonds individually: the exon-intron bond at the donor site, the intron-exon bond at the acceptor site, and the bond between the two joined exons after successful exon ligation to yield product RNA (Figure 2A left, Appendix).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Synthesis of the donor and acceptor bonds reflects precursor RNA synthesis.
source: Synthesis of the donor and acceptor bonds reflects precursor RNA synthesis.
evidence: This is a definition used in the modeling approach.

claim: Cleavage of the donor bond is caused by either splicing or by precursor RNA degradation.
source: Cleavage of the donor bond is caused by either splicing or by precursor RNA degradation.
evidence: This is a definition used in the modeling approach.

claim: The half-life of donor bonds that get spliced depends on intronic transcription at least up to the branchpoint and on the first transesterification step.
source: The half-life of those donor bonds that get spliced depends on intronic transcription at least up to the branchpoint and on the first transesterification step.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the donor bond half-life represents.

claim: Cleavage of the acceptor bond is caused by either splicing or by precursor RNA degradation.
source: Cleavage of the acceptor bond is caused by either splicing or by precursor RNA degradation.
evidence: This is a definition used in the modeling approach.

claim: The half-life of acceptor bonds that get spliced is determined by the first and the second transesterification step but not by intronic transcription.
source: The half-life of those acceptor bonds that get spliced is determined by the first and the second transesterification step but not by intronic transcription.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the acceptor bond half-life represents.

claim: Synthesis of the junction bond is the outcome of completed splicing.
source: Synthesis of the junction bond is the outcome of completed splicing.
evidence: This is a definition used in the modeling approach.

claim: Cleavage of the junction bond indicates RNA degradation.
source: Cleavage of the junction bond indicates RNA degradation (Materials and methods, Appendix).
evidence: This is a definition used in the modeling approach.

claim: Labeled and unlabeled spike-ins were injected at constant concentrations in all samples prior to the purification step.
source: Our experimental design includes the injection of labeled and unlabeled spike-ins at constant concentrations in all samples, prior to the purification step.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Spike-ins allowed for estimating the variations in sequencing depth as well as the overall newly synthesized RNA fraction of every sample.
source: These spike-ins allowed for estimating the variations in sequencing depth as well as the overall newly synthesized RNA fraction of every sample (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the purpose of the spike-ins in the experimental design.

claim: Unlabeled spike-ins allowed estimating the amount of cross-contamination of unlabeled RNAs that are purified.
source: The unlabeled spike-ins also allowed estimating the amount of cross-contamination, that is of unlabeled RNAs that are purified and which can represent a large fraction of all RNA-seq reads at short labeling durations (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes another purpose of the spike-ins in the experimental design.

claim: The study fitted the abundance of 162,134 donor, 177,543 acceptor and 156,825 junction bonds with a first-order kinetic model.
source: Using these considerations, we fitted the abundance of each of these three types of bonds with a first-order kinetic model for a total of 162,134 donor, 177,543 acceptor and 156,825 junction bonds that showed at least 100 supporting reads across the full dataset (Figure 2A right, Materials and methods, Appendix).
evidence: This describes the scope of the kinetic modeling analysis.

claim: TT-seq read counts agreed with the expected counts of the kinetic model.
source: Overall, TT-seq read counts agreed with the expected counts of our kinetic model (Figure 2A central column, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the fit shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The synthesis rates for donors and acceptors, and the product half-life inferred from distinct splice junctions agreed well.
source: The synthesis rates for donors and acceptors, and the product half-life inferred from distinct splice junctions (Materials and methods) agreed well, demonstrating the robustness of our approach (Spearman rank correlation >0.33 for synthesis time downstream of the first exon, p<2 × 10−16 and Spearman rank correlation >0.76 for half-life, p<2 × 10−16, variation of 180% fold for synthesis rate, and 32% fold for half-life, Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Extensive simulations were conducted to assess the performance and limitations of the fitting procedure.
source: We furthermore conducted extensive simulations to assess the performance and limitations of the fitting procedure to estimate the rates when the ground truth is known.
evidence: This describes validation of the modeling approach through simulations.

claim: The method leads to unbiased estimates of ground truth synthesis rates based on simulated data.
source: Based on simulated data, our method leads to unbiased estimates of ground truth synthesis rates (Appendix 1—figure 12), splicing half-time and half-life time (Appendix 1—figure 13) with high precision compared to the dynamic range.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in the Appendix.

claim: Lowering the total read coverage cut-off below 100 reads would lead to relative errors typically surpassing 100%.
source: These simulations showed that lowering the total read coverage cut-off below 100 reads would lead to relative errors typically surpassing 100% (median, Appendix 1—figure 23).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in the Appendix.

claim: Estimations of half-lives shorter than 1 min or longer than 3 days would lead to median error surpassing 100%.
source: These simulations also showed that estimations of half-lives shorter or much longer than our labeling durations (shorter than 1 min or longer than 3 days) would lead to median error surpassing 100% (Appendix 1—figure 24).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in the Appendix.

claim: The analyzed bonds mapped to 8,770 mRNAs, 162 antisense RNAs, 204 long intergenic non-coding RNAs, and 290 other non-coding RNAs based on GENCODE annotation.
source: Based on GENCODE annotation, the analyzed bonds mapped to 8,770 mRNAs, 162 RNAs antisense to protein-coding genes (asRNA), 204 long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNA), and 290 other non-coding RNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the classification of analyzed transcripts.

claim: Synthesis rates and half-lives of donors and acceptors ranged over two orders of magnitude when averaged within major isoforms.
source: When averaged within major isoforms (Materials and methods), synthesis rates and half-lives of donors and acceptors ranged over two orders of magnitude (42-fold and 48-fold change, 90% equi-tailed range), whereas the junction bond half-life spanned only slightly over one order of magnitude (8.1-fold 90% equi-tailed range, Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the distributions shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The junction bond half-life spanned slightly over one order of magnitude (8.1-fold 90% equi-tailed range) when averaged within major isoforms.
source: When averaged within major isoforms (Materials and methods), synthesis rates and half-lives of donors and acceptors ranged over two orders of magnitude (42-fold and 48-fold change, 90% equi-tailed range), whereas the junction bond half-life spanned only slightly over one order of magnitude (8.1-fold 90% equi-tailed range, Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the distributions shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Major isoform aggregated rates generally agreed with previously reported splicing rates and RNA half-lives.
source: These major isoform aggregated rates generally agreed with previously reported splicing rates and RNA half-lives (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Mukherjee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous studies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mRNAs were spliced significantly faster (median of 7.2 min) than lincRNAs (median of 11 min).
source: Moreover, mRNAs were spliced significantly faster (median of 7.2 min) than lincRNAs (median of 11 min, p<2 × 10−16) and other non-coding RNAs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mRNAs had junction bonds with the longest half-lives (median of 316 min).
source: Also, mRNAs had junction bonds with the longest half-lives (median of 316 min) (Figure 2D), consistent with previous studies (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Schlackow et al., 2017; Schwalb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: The obtained apparent splicing times in the range of minutes agree with many previous estimates obtained using different methods.
source: The obtained apparent splicing times in the range of minutes agree with many previous estimates that were obtained using different methods, but argue against fast splicing, within less than a minute, that was suggested by some studies (Carmo-Fonseca and Kirchhausen, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results with previous literature.

claim: The results argue against fast splicing within less than a minute.
source: The obtained apparent splicing times in the range of minutes agree with many previous estimates that were obtained using different methods, but argue against fast splicing, within less than a minute, that was suggested by some studies (Carmo-Fonseca and Kirchhausen, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed splicing times in the range of minutes.

claim: The de novo annotation of introns is in agreement with a minimal intron length of about 80 nt.
source: First, our de novo annotation of introns is in agreement with a minimal intron length of about 80 nt (Figure 3A), as expected from the spatial needs within the spliceosome (Ruskin et al., 1985; Wieringa et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Among introns shorter than 2,000 nt, acceptor and donor bond half-life showed similar distributions and decreased with increasing intron length.
source: Second, we find that among introns shorter than 2,000 nt, acceptor and donor bond half-life showed similar distributions and decreased with increasing intron length (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Among introns longer than 2,000 nt, acceptor bond half-life plateaued at a median value of about 4 min.
source: Among introns longer than 2,000 nt, acceptor bond half-life plateaued at a median value of about 4 min, whereas donor bond half-life increased with intron length up to a median value of about 8 min for introns larger than 7,700 nt (last septile).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of intron length effects on bond half-lives.

claim: Among introns longer than 2,000 nt, donor bond half-life increased with intron length up to a median value of about 8 min for introns larger than 7,700 nt.
source: Among introns longer than 2,000 nt, acceptor bond half-life plateaued at a median value of about 4 min, whereas donor bond half-life increased with intron length up to a median value of about 8 min for introns larger than 7,700 nt (last septile).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of intron length effects on bond half-lives.

claim: Donor sites of long introns are transcribed much earlier than acceptor sites and splicing can only start when the intron is transcribed.
source: A possible explanation for this significant difference is that donor sites of long introns are transcribed much earlier than acceptor sites and splicing can only start when the intron is transcribed.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed difference between donor and acceptor bond half-lives for long introns.

claim: Very few introns violated the predicted limit of donor bond half-life based on a maximum polymerase elongation velocity of 4 kb/min.
source: Assuming a maximum polymerase elongation velocity of 4 kb/min (Fuchs et al., 2014; Gressel et al., 2017; Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Saponaro et al., 2014; Veloso et al., 2014), we observed very few introns violating this predicted limit (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous studies on elongation velocity.

claim: For shorter introns, the donor bond half-life and the acceptor bond half-life were similar, indicating that the second transesterification step is fast compared to the overall splicing kinetics.
source: For shorter introns, the donor bond half-life and the acceptor bond half-life were similar (Figure 3B), indicating that the second transesterification step is fast compared to the overall splicing kinetics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of donor and acceptor bond half-lives for short introns.

claim: The median half-life was 2.5-fold longer for donor bonds than for acceptor bonds of first introns.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the median half-life was 2.5-fold (p<2×10−16) longer for donor bonds than for acceptor bonds of first introns (Figure 3D), which are known to be more slowly transcribed (Danko et al., 2013; Fuchs et al., 2014; Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Saponaro et al., 2014; Veloso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous studies on transcription of first introns.

claim: First introns are known to be more slowly transcribed.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the median half-life was 2.5-fold (p<2×10−16) longer for donor bonds than for acceptor bonds of first introns (Figure 3D), which are known to be more slowly transcribed (Danko et al., 2013; Fuchs et al., 2014; Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Saponaro et al., 2014; Veloso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A small significant difference in half-life was found for the last intron (1.4-fold), which could reflect slower polymerases near the transcript end or different kinetics of splicing of the last intron.
source: A small significant difference was also found for the last intron (1.4-fold, p<2×10−16), which could reflect slower polymerases near the transcript end or different kinetics of splicing of the last intron (Davis-Turak et al., 2015; Rigo and Martinson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous studies, with speculation about the reasons.

claim: Donor half-life and thus the beginning of splicing is limited by transcription elongation for long introns.
source: In conclusion, these data show that donor half-life and thus the beginning of splicing is limited by transcription elongation for long introns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of intron length effects on donor bond half-lives.

claim: The length of the intron influences splicing kinetics in at least two different ways.
source: Taken together, our results are generally consistent with the co-transcriptional nature of splicing and reveal that the length of the intron influences splicing kinetics in at least two different ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of intron length effects.

claim: A linear model was built to estimate changes in donor bond half-life as a function of single nucleotide changes relative to the consensus sequence.
source: To gain insights into the sequence determinants for splicing, we built a linear model (Materials and methods) that allowed us to estimate changes in donor bond half-life as a function of single nucleotide changes relative to the consensus sequence.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used to analyze sequence effects.

claim: The single nucleotide model could explain 19% of the observed variance in log-transformed donor bond half-life.
source: The single nucleotide model could explain 19% of the observed variance in log-transformed donor bond half-life and achieved a median relative error for individual sites of 150%, which is small compared to the dynamic range across sites spanning two orders of magnitude (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the model performance shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nucleotide deviations from the consensus splice-site increase donor bond half-life.
source: This analysis showed that nucleotide deviations from the consensus splice-site increase donor bond half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the single nucleotide model analysis.

claim: These findings are consistent with evolutionary pressure for donor sequences optimized for fast splicing.
source: These findings are consistent with evolutionary pressure for donor sequences optimized for fast splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deviations from consensus slow splicing.

claim: Substitution of the highly frequent G at +1 or −1 from the donor site with a C resulted in an increase in bond half-life.
source: In our model, substitution of the highly frequent G at +1 or −1 from the donor site with a C resulted in an increase in bond half-life (Figure 4B), likely because C cannot form a stable interaction with a C in the U1 snRNA, in agreement with previous in vitro studies (Kondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the model results shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous studies.

claim: At position +3 from the donor site, a change from A to G has only a minor effect on the bond half-life, likely because G can still form a non-canonical base pair with U in the U1 snRNA.
source: In contrast, at position +3 from the donor site, a change from A to G has only a minor effect on the bond half-life (Figure 4B), likely because G can still form a non-canonical base pair with U in the U1 snRNA (Kondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the model results shown in Figure 4B and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Interactions of the precursor RNA donor region with U1 snRNA contribute to the observed donor bond half-lives.
source: These results suggest that interactions of the precursor RNA donor region with U1 snRNA contribute to the observed donor bond half-lives.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between predicted nucleotide effects and known U1 snRNA interactions.

claim: U5 interactions may contribute to the kinetics of donor cleavage.
source: Our results suggest that U5 interactions may contribute to the kinetics of donor cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between predicted nucleotide effects and known U5 snRNA interactions.

claim: An A in the position −3 relative to the donor site leads to faster donor bond half-life supposedly because this enables base-pairing with U5 snRNA in the extended precursor RNA-U5 snRNA duplex.
source: For example, an A in the position −3 relative to the donor site leads to faster donor bond half-life supposedly because this enables base-pairing with U5 snRNA in the extended precursor RNA-U5 snRNA duplex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and known U5 snRNA interactions.

claim: Interactions in the C* complex were predictive of donor bond half-life.
source: We also found that interactions in the C* complex were predictive of donor bond half-life (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis correlating nucleotide effects with C* complex interactions.

claim: Changes in the branchpoint adenine and at all positions −4 to +3 of the branchpoint show kinetic effects, except for the positions −1 and +2.
source: In particular, changes in the branchpoint adenine and at all positions −4 to +3 of the branchpoint show kinetic effects, except for the positions −1 and +2 that are predicted to not contribute to donor bond half-life (grey highlighting in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the model results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Positions −1 and +2 relative to the branchpoint are the only two nucleotides in the vicinity of the branchpoint that do not interact with U2 in the C* complex.
source: In agreement with the structural data, these nucleotides are also the only two nucleotides in the vicinity of the branchpoint that do not interact with U2 in the C* complex (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to structural data.

claim: The precursor RNA nucleotides interacting with snRNAs during 5' splice site recognition showed the strongest effects on donor bond half-life.
source: When compared to each other, the precursor RNA nucleotides interacting with snRNAs during 5' splice site recognition showed the strongest effects on donor bond half-life, followed by nucleotides interacting in the B complex, and to a lesser extent the nucleotides interacting in the C* complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Positions with no predicted contact in spliceosome structures showed least effects on donor bond half-life.
source: Positions with no predicted contact in these structures showed least effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A regression model predicting log-transformed acceptor bond half-life from sequence explained 20% of variance with a median relative error of 150%.
source: We also built a regression model predicting log-transformed acceptor bond half-life from sequence (Figure 5B, 20% of variance explained, median relative error of 150%).
evidence: This is supported by the model performance shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Single nucleotide changes around the acceptor site generally had larger effects on acceptor bond half-life, reflecting effects on step two kinetics.
source: Single nucleotide changes around the acceptor site generally had larger effects on acceptor bond half-life, reflecting effects on step two kinetics, whereas changes around the donor site had greater effects on donor bond half-life, reflecting effects on step one kinetics (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of nucleotide effects shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nucleotide changes that influence base pair interactions reported for the P-complex in S. cerevisiae showed stronger effects on the acceptor bond half-life than for the donor bond half-life.
source: Nevertheless, nucleotide changes that influence base pair interactions reported for the P-complex in S. cerevisiae (Bai et al., 2017) showed stronger effects on the acceptor bond half-life than for the donor bond half-life (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and a citation to the yeast P-complex structure.

claim: A non-canonical G branchpoint does not affect acceptor bond half-life but increases donor bond half-life.
source: Our results indicate that a non-canonical G branchpoint does not affect acceptor bond half-life but increases donor bond half-life.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of nucleotide effects on donor and acceptor bond half-lives.

claim: The predominant G at the donor −1 nucleotide leads to fast donor cleavage kinetics but to slow acceptor cleavage kinetics.
source: We also observed that the predominant G at the donor −1 nucleotide leads to fast donor cleavage kinetics but to slow acceptor cleavage kinetics, maybe because this interferes with positioning of the neighboring +1 donor nucleotide that serves as a nucleophile during step two.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of nucleotide effects, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The donor −1 position is predominantly G, presumably because this improves donor site recognition by base pairing with a C in U1 snRNA.
source: Despite this disadvantage in acceptor cleavage kinetics, the donor −1 position is predominantly G, presumably because this improves donor site recognition by base pairing with a C in U1 snRNA as described above.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed sequence preference and known U1 snRNA interactions.

claim: Splicing is modulated by auxiliary factors, including serine/arginine-rich proteins and hnRNPs, that bind to regulatory motifs around the splice sites.
source: Splicing is modulated by auxiliary factors, including serine/arginine-rich proteins and hnRNPs (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins), that bind to regulatory motifs around the splice sites (Fu and Ares, 2014; Matlin et al., 2005; Wang and Burge, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Extended models for donor and acceptor bond half-life including single nucleotide effects and all 65,536 possible RNA octamers in four extended intronic regions were derived.
source: We derived two extended models for donor and acceptor bond half-life including the single nucleotide effects in the core regions investigated so far and all 65,536 possible RNA octamers in four extended intronic regions, 100 nt downstream of the donor site, 100 nt upstream of the acceptor site, and 100 nt upstream of the branchpoint and the region between branchpoint and acceptor site (Figure 6A, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the extended modeling approach.

claim: Feature selection yielded 551 octamers jointly predicting donor bond half-life and 2,319 octamers jointly predicting acceptor bond half-life.
source: Because of the very large number of octamers, we used a feature selection method (Lasso regression), which yielded 551 octamers jointly predicting donor bond half-life and 2,319 octamers jointly predicting acceptor bond half-life (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the results of the feature selection analysis.

claim: The extended models substantially increased the proportion of variance explained from 19% to 26% for the log-transformed donor bond half-life and from 20% to 29% for the log-transformed acceptor bond half-life.
source: Compared to the single nucleotide models, the extended models substantially increased the proportion of variance explained from 19% to 26% for the log-transformed donor bond half-life and from 20% to 29% for the log-transformed acceptor bond half-life (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the model performance shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The improved prediction of the extended models over the single nucleotide models is mostly attributable to the octamers of the extended intronic regions.
source: The improved prediction of the extended models over the single nucleotide models is mostly attributable to the octamers of the extended intronic regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of model performances.

claim: The largest number of predictive octamers identified by the donor bond half-life model was found in the 5' donor site region.
source: The largest number of predictive octamers identified by the donor bond half-life model was found in the 5' donor site region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the acceptor bond half-life model, the regions flanking the branchpoint and acceptor site contained most predictive octamers.
source: In the acceptor bond half-life model, the regions flanking the branchpoint and acceptor site contained most predictive octamers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and associated with largest proportion of variance explained (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6C.

claim: The effects of octamers on bond half-life were of similar order of magnitude than the effects of single nucleotides in donor, acceptor and branchpoint sites.
source: Moreover, the effects of octamers on bond half-life were of similar order of magnitude than the effects of single nucleotides in donor, acceptor and branchpoint sites for both categories (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, median effect for octamer 1.4%, median effect for nucleotide 5.4%).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 258 octamers predicted by the donor bond half-life model associated with 69 RNA-binding proteins.
source: We found 258 octamers predicted by the donor bond half-life model (47% versus 42% of non-selected octamers, p=0.017, Fisher test) associating with 69 RNA-binding proteins and 1,039 octamers identified by the acceptor bond half-life model (45% versus 42% of non-selected octamers, p=0.007, Fisher test) associating with 99 RNA-binding proteins motifs (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, relative position weight matrix score >0.9 and selecting for the 5% highest absolute scores, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis matching octamers to the ATtRACT database.

claim: 1,039 octamers identified by the acceptor bond half-life model associated with 99 RNA-binding proteins motifs.
source: We found 258 octamers predicted by the donor bond half-life model (47% versus 42% of non-selected octamers, p=0.017, Fisher test) associating with 69 RNA-binding proteins and 1,039 octamers identified by the acceptor bond half-life model (45% versus 42% of non-selected octamers, p=0.007, Fisher test) associating with 99 RNA-binding proteins motifs (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, relative position weight matrix score >0.9 and selecting for the 5% highest absolute scores, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis matching octamers to the ATtRACT database.

claim: Several serine/arginine-rich and hnRNP proteins regulate donor and acceptor bond half-life in both positive and negative fashions, depending on the location of their binding site.
source: Our results suggest that several serine/arginine-rich and hnRNP proteins (Supplementary file 5) regulate donor and acceptor bond half-life in both positive and negative fashions, depending on the location of their binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the octamer analysis and matching to RNA-binding protein motifs.

claim: Octamers associated with the binding site of Ptpb1 are predictive of short donor bond half-life when present between branchpoint and acceptor site but they prolong the donor bond half-life when located near the donor site.
source: Octamers associated with the binding site of the polypyrimidine tract-binding protein Ptpb1 are predictive of short donor bond half-life when present between branchpoint and acceptor site but they prolong the donor bond half-life when located near the donor site (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Octamers predicted to affect donor or acceptor bond half-life show significantly higher phylogenetic conservation compared to random octamers, except for octamers in the region 100 nt downstream of the donor site for donor bond half-life.
source: Except for octamers predicted to affect donor bond half-life in the region 100 nt downstream of the donor site, the remaining ones show significantly higher phylogenetic conservation compared to a negative control of random octamers (Figure 6E), providing evidence of their biological significance.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic conservation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The 'splicing yield' is defined as the proportion of precursor RNA successfully converted into spliced RNA.
source: To account for this, we defined the 'splicing yield' as the proportion of precursor RNA successfully converted into spliced RNA (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a definition introduced by the authors.

claim: A splicing yield of 1 means that all precursor RNAs that are synthesized are also successfully spliced.
source: A splicing yield of 1 means that all precursor RNAs that are synthesized are also successfully spliced, whereas a splicing yield less than one means that only a fraction of the precursor RNA is converted to spliced product.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the splicing yield metric.

claim: The splicing yield across sites was much higher for mRNAs (median = 1.2) than for antisense RNAs (median = 0.2), lincRNAs (median = 0.3), and other non-coding RNAs (median = 0.5).
source: We found that the splicing yield across sites was much higher for mRNAs (median = 1.2, Figure 7B) than for antisense RNAs (median = 0.2), lincRNAs (median = 0.3), and other non-coding RNAs (median = 0.5), suggesting that degradation pathways are competing with splicing more intensively for non-coding RNAs than for coding RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Degradation pathways are competing with splicing more intensively for non-coding RNAs than for coding RNAs.
source: We found that the splicing yield across sites was much higher for mRNAs (median = 1.2, Figure 7B) than for antisense RNAs (median = 0.2), lincRNAs (median = 0.3), and other non-coding RNAs (median = 0.5), suggesting that degradation pathways are competing with splicing more intensively for non-coding RNAs than for coding RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in splicing yield between RNA classes.

claim: Introns targeted by the minor spliceosome showed two-fold slower donor and acceptor bond half-lives compared to those targeted by the major spliceosome.
source: Although introns targeted by the minor spliceosome showed two-fold slower donor and acceptor bond half-lives compared to those targeted by the major spliceosome (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), the minor spliceosome nonetheless reached similar splicing yields.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A model was built to predict splicing yield based on sequence.
source: To analyze how the nature of the splice sites contributes to splicing yield, we built a model that allow us to predict splicing yield based on sequence (Figure 7E).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for splicing yield.

claim: Deviations from the consensus sequence led to lower splicing yield.
source: Similar to the effects on bond half-lives (Figure 4B, Figure 5C), deviations from the consensus sequence led to lower splicing yield.
evidence: This is supported by the model results for splicing yield.

claim: Nucleotides near a splice site showed stronger effects on splicing yield than more distant ones, suggesting that the early recognition of donor and acceptor splice sites is a determinant for splicing yield.
source: Furthermore, nucleotides near a splice site showed stronger effects than more distant ones, suggesting that the early recognition of donor and acceptor splice sites is a determinant for splicing yield.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of nucleotide effects on splicing yield.

claim: Rate and yield are distinct aspects of splicing that may have evolved independently.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that rate and yield are distinct aspects of splicing that may have evolved independently and that the sequence around splice sites determines both the rate and the yield of splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of splicing yield and its relationship to splicing kinetics.

claim: The sequence around splice sites determines both the rate and the yield of splicing.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that rate and yield are distinct aspects of splicing that may have evolved independently and that the sequence around splice sites determines both the rate and the yield of splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence-based models of both rate and yield.
